Ophthalmology · published research

Color contrast sensitivity

A small repeated-measures study reported improved cone-mediated color-contrast thresholds for about one week after three minutes of morning 670 nm light. Two other studies reported visual-function changes after indirect thoracic or broad-spectrum light exposure and are not direct ocular PBM trials.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A small repeated-measures study reported improved cone-mediated color-contrast thresholds for about one week after three minutes of morning 670 nm light. Two other studies reported visual-function changes after indirect thoracic or broad-spectrum light exposure and are not direct ocular PBM trials.

Summary of the Evidence

Three unique human titles appear under the database spelling Colour contrast sensitivity. Only one tested direct ocular PBM. A 2025 study used thoracic near-infrared exposure with eyes shielded, and a 2026 study evaluated broad-spectrum light exposure; these are narrowly related mappings rather than direct ocular PBM trials. No animal or laboratory study was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

Shinhmar and colleagues studied a brief 670 nm visible red-light exposure in older adults. A single three-minute morning exposure improved cone-mediated color-contrast thresholds for about one week; an afternoon exposure did not show the same result. The study was small and repeated-measures, not a blinded sham-controlled clinical trial. Jeffery and colleagues reported visual-function changes after thoracic 830 to 860 nm near-infrared exposure with the eyes shielded, while Barrett and Jeffery studied broad-spectrum light spanning 400 to 1500 nm. Neither is a direct ocular PBM replication (Shinhmar et al. 2021 Jeffery et al. 2025 Barrett & Jeffery 2026).

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone laboratory study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The direct study used 670 nm red visible light for three minutes in the morning. The related thoracic protocol used near-infrared light while the eyes were shielded; the broad-spectrum study used a much wider visible-to-infrared range. These routes and spectra test different exposures and should not be combined as one ocular dose.

Interpretation

The direct study reports a short-term visual-function change after morning red light. Durability beyond about one week, clinical importance, and reproducibility under blinded sham control remain uncertain.

Evidence strength in source summaryShort-term color-contrast thresholds after direct morning red-light exposure: Low Indirect thoracic or broad-spectrum light exposure: Very low
Publications and records3 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Three small human studies were identified, but only one used direct ocular PBM. That repeated-measures study reported a short-lived improvement after morning exposure; the other studies used shielded-eye thoracic light or broad-spectrum ambient exposure. Blinded sham-controlled replication with direct ocular treatment is needed.
